name: Resistance bands
lead: Resistance bands are elastic bands, loops or tubes, usually latex, rubber or fabric-covered, used for strength training and rehabilitation. Their tension rises as they are stretched, they are sold in graded and often colour-coded strengths, and they weigh little, which makes them easy to store and carry [1][2].

Wikipedia traces their origin to the early 20th century, when surgical tubing was used for muscle rehabilitation, and notes that they are now used widely in general fitness [1]. Grokipedia dates standardised colour-coded bands to the Thera-Band line introduced by the Hygenic Corporation in 1976 [2]. Common types include flat bands, looped mini-bands or superbands, and tube bands with handles [2].

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis found that elastic resistance training produced strength gains similar to conventional resistance training [15]. In appearance-oriented training, bands are used both for muscle building at home and for posture-oriented exercises such as face pulls, pull-aparts and external rotations. Evidence comparing bands with weights for appearance outcomes specifically is limited.

paras: Wikipedia notes that bands are typically colour-coded by resistance level, although the colour codes vary between brands, and that they come as loops, as tubing without handles, or as tubing with clip-on or fixed handles [1]. Grokipedia describes standard flat bands that can be tied into loops, looped mini-bands used for lower-body and glute activation, and tube bands with handles used for upper-body presses and pulls [2]. Resistance levels range from light to heavy, and users adjust difficulty by choosing a thicker band, repetitions or the band's stretch length [1][2].

A band provides elastic resistance: the force required increases with how far it is stretched, so resistance is lowest at the start of a movement and highest at the end of the range [2]. Wikipedia lists the band's resistance and the number of repetitions as the main variables for adjusting intensity [1].

Scales have been proposed to estimate intensity with bands, including validation studies of the OMNI-Resistance Exercise Scale of perceived exertion with Thera-Band bands and of a resistance intensity scale for Thera-Band elastic bands [3][4]. Because resistance depends on band length, anchoring and stretch, tracking progressive overload is generally less exact than with plates.

The 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis published in SAGE Open Medicine concluded that elastic resistance training produced similar strength gains to conventional resistance training [15]. Wikipedia reports that a 2014 study found a bench press and a resistance band push-up at similar stress levels produced similar strength gains [1].

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of resistance exercise forms in overweight and obese adults, covering 15 studies and 669 participants, compared body weight, resistance bands and free weights. It reported that resistance bands improved body fat more than the other training types in this population, while body-weight training was better for increasing skeletal muscle mass [5]. A 2022 meta-analysis of resistance band exercise in frail older adults reported that it reduced frailty after 24 weeks [6]. These populations differ from healthy people training for appearance.

For muscle growth, a 2021 network meta-analysis of resistance-training load reported broadly similar hypertrophy across a wide range of loads, with heavier loads favouring maximal strength [7]. Whether bands are equivalent to weights for hypertrophy in trained people is less clear from the sources reviewed, and the claim that bands are superior to weights is not supported by them.

Bands can snap or slip if nicked, overstretched or poorly anchored, and recoil to the face or eye is a recognised injury mechanism. Latex bands can trigger allergic reactions in people with latex allergy, and non-latex alternatives exist. A 2024 BMJ note on tendinopathy lists weights and resistance bands among recommended exercise approaches for that condition, indicating their use in clinical rehabilitation [8].

In fitness and appearance communities, bands are discussed in two roles: a cheap alternative for building muscle at home or when travelling, and posture work for the upper back and rotator cuff to counter a rounded-shoulder look. Threads such as 'Is resistance band that effective?' on r/workout and 'Do resistance bands build muscle?' on a LiveScience forum show recurring questions on whether bands can replace weights [9][10]. The site's own rating reflects that bands can build muscle but are not presented as superior to weights.

Most clinical studies of resistance bands have been done in clinical populations rather than in healthy people training for appearance. These include a 2022 meta-analysis in frail older adults [6]; a 2021 meta-analysis of resistance training forms in overweight and obese adults [5]; a randomized trial of ankle strengthening using eccentric, concentric and resistance-band programmes in 63 sedentary young men [11]; a review of minimal-equipment pulmonary rehabilitation programmes for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [13]; and a randomized pilot trial of a group strength and flexibility programme in long-term care residents [14]. A 2019 meta-analysis directly compared elastic and conventional resistance training for strength [15].
